div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: A recent survey of industry practices by Akesson et al. [1] indicates that the use of response-time analysis (RTA) is surprisingly limited. In particular, in response to Question 23 of Akesson et al.'s survey, the majority of respondents (61%) indicated that the presence of potential deadline violations is assessed by running tests and checking for overruns. In contrast, the use of in-house schedulability analyses or commerciallyavailable schedulability tools is far less widespread (31% and 9%, respectively).

As RTA is a well-researched and practical technique, one may expect it to be applied far more widely. In particular, in the context of soft and firm real-time systems, which represent the majority of the systems covered by Akesson et al.'s survey [1], the use of measurement-based techniques for parameter estimation -such as each task's worst-case execution time (WCET) -is acceptable. Once all parameters are known, applying one of the many RTAs available in the literature is conceptually straightforward. However, as Akesson et al.'s results indicate, the barriers to adoption in practice remain high.

Major factors contributing to this barrier are without a doubt the expertise and effort required to actually conduct an RTA. Especially when considering commodity platforms such as Linux, engineers are typically domain experts focusing on the application they are building, and cannot be expected to have a thorough understanding of the latest applicable scheduling theory. It is also not reasonable to expect engineers to manually piece together a measurement-based RTA from low-level tracing toolkits and various academic analysis tools or libraries. Unfortunately, however, no automated, end-to-end solution exists.

To fill this gap, and to demonstrate that fully automatic RTA is possible, for practical workloads and without requiring specialized knowledge on behalf of the user, we are developing DMXTRACE (Dynamic Model eXTractor for Response-time Analysis from Collected Events), a user-space RTA tool for Linux that works on unmodified kernels for arbitrary tasks.

DMXTRACE seeks to lift the burden of matching system configurations, tracing task parameters, and identifying applicable RTAs from the user. The tool detects the system's configuration and extracts a timing model of its workload, matches the observations with one of a number of supported system models from the literature, and finally picks the most precise applicable analysis. Model parameters are estimated by tracing kernel events using Linux's FTRACE facility. As threads are treated as "black boxes," DMXTRACE does not require access to source code, nor does it require the user to provide any static information about the workload.

DMXTRACE runs directly on the target system. Its intended use cases include serving as a development aid (e.g., to debug timing issues or to assess specification compliance), as a system monitor during testing (e.g., integration or regression testing, or performance tuning), and as a runtime monitor in deployment (e.g., to notice and gracefully react to unexpected overload). DMXTRACE is not constrained to specific workloads: for well-behaved workloads (e.g., periodic activations), it identifies all model parameters required for analysis (e.g., period, release jitter, and offset); in case of irregular activation patterns, the tool instead models the load with a request-bound function (RBF) [2].

DMXTRACE is still in an early stage of development, with support for threads scheduled under fixed-priority partitioned scheduling as a proof of concept. In this paper, we report on key challenges, the tool's design, our ongoing development, and the proposed mechanism for task parameter extraction.

div.head: II. DESIGN AND CHALLENGES
div.p: The primary goal of DMXTRACE is to lower the entry barrier imposed by the need for real-time expertise. To this end, we define three requirements that drove our design decisions and the construction of the tool. a) Ease of use. The need for specialized expertise is one of the major obstacles in the adoption of RTA. Therefore, the tool must be fully automated and require no real-time knowledge. b) No ad-hoc kernel patches. Many application developers are not willing to patch the kernel. Therefore, the tool should not require an ad-hoc kernel patch to work, and must instead run on a stock Linux kernel (or, optionally, its widespread PREEMPT RT variant). c) Practicality. DMXTRACE must ultimately yield useful information about the system. To this end, we are willing to trade accuracy to support a wide range of real-world workloads.

Meeting the above requirements is not an easy task, especially in the context of Linux. In this section, we first present the general architecture of DMXTRACE and then discuss the various challenges encountered in its design and implementation.

div.head: A. DMXTRACE architecture
div.p: The three aforementioned requirements lead to the design illustrated in Fig. 1. The tool consists of four self-contained modules, which can conceptually be divided into two parts: monitoring and analysis. In the following we give a brief description of each of these modules.

The configuration monitor is in charge of extracting system parameters describing the system configuration. Such parameters are related to Linux-specific mechanisms (e.g., processor placement and scheduling policies) or hardware features (e.g., processor topology and heterogeneous processors).

The event tracer monitors the activity of real-time threads. This activity is represented by a trace of scheduling events (i.e., changes in the state of the thread). We are tracing five types of event: activation (sleeping to runnable), dispatch (runnable to running), preemption (running to runnable), deactivation (running to sleeping), and exit (thread terminated). Scheduling events are traced using the FTRACE facility that is integrated in the mainline of the kernel. As a result, tracing does not require an ad-hoc kernel patch, as specified by requirement (b).

The model extractor takes as input a set of traces and a set of system parameters and, for each trace, it derives a timing model that explains the behavior of the corresponding thread. The output is a system model, which comprises a set of extracted timing models (one per thread) and the system parameters. The model extractor supports different timing models, including RBFs that can be extracted regardless of the task behavior. This allows DMXTRACE to support a wide variety of workloads, respecting requirement (c). The model extraction module is described in further detail in Section III.

The response-time analyzer produces response-time bounds based on the system model. It chooses and performs the most appropriate supported analysis (i.e., the one that produces the tighter bounds). Since the choice of analysis is automated, no expertise is required from the user, making DMXTRACE widely accessible, in the spirit of requirement (a).

div.head: B. Design and Implementation Challenges
div.p: Since the design of Linux is not real-time oriented, there is a mismatch between the concepts of the real-time literature and the ones of Linux. This fact is at the root of the following challenges we are facing in the development of DMXTRACE. Impact of system parameters. The system parameters extracted by the configuration monitor have an influence both on the model extraction and the response-time analysis. A key challenge is to map these parameters to the corresponding concepts of the real-time literature, if they are related.

System parameters can be split into three categories: (i) hardware features that render the system less predictable, such as hyperthreading, which renders execution times less predictable (but can be disabled); (ii) Linux features that do not affect the applicable analysis, such as kernel threads, which can be identified and accounted for; and finally (iii) Linux features that affect the applicable analysis, such as processor placement (i.e., affinity masks), scheduling policies (SCHED FIFO, SCHED RR), and real-time throttling (i.e., a limit on the share of processor time for fixed-priority real-time threads).

If some system parameter prevents an analysis from being applied, or some timing model from being extracted, then the tool reports a diagnostic of the problem so that the system can be appropriately tuned.

Identifying job boundaries. In the real-time systems literature, recurring activities of a system are modeled by tasks releasing jobs. Unfortunately, Linux has no notion of job and task, providing instead a thread abstraction. This poses a fundamental challenge for the model extraction: how can we identify distinct jobs in a trace describing a thread execution?

A common approach to implement jobs in Linux is to have blocks of execution with run-to-completion semantics separated by blocking system calls -for instance, a sequence of computations separated by a call to clock_nanosleep(). Within this structure, jobs are separated by deactivations, allowing us to clearly identify job boundaries in the trace.

However, it is not always the case that real-world programs follow this simple structure -in fact, what defines a job is entirely application-dependent. For example, a job could be also the processing of a network packet or a computation offloaded to an hardware accelerator. Therefore, in general, there is no universal boundary between jobs on Linux.

A common ground is that job endings always correspond to a deactivation (unless a job completes after the arrival of the next, in which case there is no suspension between the two jobs). However, the converse is not true: between deactivations representing job endings there could be other deactivations (e.g., caused by read/write system calls). In timing models, this type of deactivation is modeled as a self-suspension [3]. Thus, a deactivation can be interpreted as a job ending or as the start of a self-suspension, making it challenging to accurately determine boundaries between jobs.

Self-suspensions are common in most Linux workloads: even a simple page fault can lead to a self-suspension. Furthermore, it is unrealistic to expect practical workloads to avoid blocking system calls or any other source of self-suspensions. Hence, to meet requirement (c), it is necessary to detect self-suspensions to find job boundaries.

Robustness to imprecision in the trace. Any thread is inherently subject to some degree of deviation from its intended execution pattern. The sources of this noise vary widely: from OS-related causes (wake-up latency and scheduling overhead) to network-induced queuing delays. This is expected in real systems, hence timing models typically use release jitter in order to model such noise.

However, even if noise is accounted for, the trace can still differ from the timing model that was intended at design time. This effect is caused by factors that have no relation with the timing model of the thread, and that represent practical concerns. An example is the initialization of programs: clearly, the initial part of the execution does not reflect the long-term behavior of the thread, and thus we discard it.

Another problem is that some events may be elided. When a new job arrives before the completion of its predecessor, the execution of the thread is not suspended, and therefore the trace does not contain a deactivation event. As a result, two or more consecutive jobs may appear in the trace as a single longer job. This scenario can be caused, for instance, by delays induced by interference from higher priority threads. The model extractor must recognize and extract noise while being robust to these elided events.
Most of the challenges exposed in this section make the model extraction particularly challenging. Next, we discuss this module in detail.

div.head: III. MODEL EXTRACTION
div.p: This section provides a high-level overview of the model extraction module. The purpose of this module is to extract a model correctly explaining the observed behavior of a thread, i.e., that is as close as possible of the ground truth. The module currently consists of three model extractors: (1) a periodic task extractor, (2) a spectral analyzer, and (3) an RBF extractor; each of those respectively extracting non selfsuspending periodic tasks with jitter and offset [4], segmented and floating self-suspending periodic task models [3], and request-bound functions.

In the vast majority of cases, a trace can be explained by several models. In order to select one, we adopt a hierarchy of models in which simpler, more restrictive models are favored over others that are more descriptive but more complex. Fig. 2 illustrates how, based on the hierarchy, the trace is sequentially processed and possible models are checked at each step. If the extraction of a model fails, DMXTRACE falls back to a more complex model, and the procedure terminates as soon as a model is successfully extracted. RBFs are used as a "catch-all case" if no other model can be matched.

In the remainder of this section, we provide further details on the three model extractors currently supported by DMX-TRACE. Then, we present preliminary experimental results for the periodic task extraction.

div.head: A. Period extraction
div.p: The simplest model DMXTRACE tries to extract is the non-self suspending task model with jitter and offset. Consider a trace of n observed activations o 1 , . . . , o n . The first step of the extraction is to identify an interval of possible periods T that can explain the observed activations. If there is no jitter, the period for two activations o j and o k , such that k = j + l, is given by the average distance between these activations.

The biggest or smallest distance between o j and o k is observed when one observation corresponds to an activation released with J max jitter and the other to an activation with no jitter at all. The interval of periods explaining all the observations in the trace o 1 , . . . , o n is given by the intersection of the intervals for all pairs j, k such that 1 ≤ j < k ≤ n. If the resulting interval is empty, then the trace is deemed as non-periodic; otherwise a period is selected from this interval.

The choice of period can affect the feasibility of some analyses, because a poor choice can lead to a large hyperperiod. To avoid this issue, we currently use a heuristic to extract round periods -specifically, we pick the multiple of 100µs closest to the middle of the feasible periods interval. This choice is based on two intuitions: first, humans tend to pick round periods, and second, the least common multiple of round numbers tends to be smaller. For non-round periods, this choice may result in a slight loss of accuracy for the RTA. However, if the analysis complexity depends on the hyperperiod (as is the case with [4]), using non-round periods likely renders the analysis impossible.

The last step is jitter and offset extraction. In this procedure, we search for an offset such that every observation is contained in exactly one period. Then, for each observed activation, we extract the jitter by comparing it with the beginning of its containing period. The offset is selected to obtain the smallest jitter. As the number of observation increases, the range of possible offsets shrinks, as does the error on the extracted jitter.

div.head: B. Spectral analysis
div.p: The procedure described in the previous section fails with traces observed from periodic self-suspending tasks. Indeed, as self-suspensions are not distinguishable from job endings, the sequence of observed activations does not necessarily follow a regular pattern. However, if the task is periodic, there is still a subset of evenly spaced activation events. We can exploit this structure to filter activations corresponding to self-suspension endings and decide whether the trace is periodic or not. To this end, we employ a spectral analysis on the trace.

Our approach to spectral analysis relies on a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to study the frequencies of activations within a trace. If a periodic subset of activations exists, then a spike is distinguishable in the frequency domain. This spike can be extracted with filtering, and used to reconstruct a periodic sequence of activations. By comparing this reconstructed sequence with the original trace, we can filter out activations due to self-suspensions and proceed to period extraction. By offering the ability to distinguish self-suspensions, this approach allows us to extract floating or segmented self-suspending task models. If no spike is detected during the frequency domain filtering, then the trace is deemed non-periodic and we fall back to RBF extraction.

The spectral analysis approach has demonstrated its applicability on synthetic traces, but an extensive study on real traces is needed. We are therefore exploring this direction to clearly identify the accuracy of the self-suspension detection and its limitations on real programs.

div.head: C. RBF extraction
div.p: If a trace is rejected by the spectral analyzer, then it does not exhibit a structure we can currently exploit for model extraction. This is an issue of particular importance, considering that this occurs quite frequently (e.g., sporadic tasks are particularly suited to model the behavior of server-based applications). Hence, in the interest of practicality (requirement (c)) it is crucial to provide support for a "catch-all case" model. Therefore, the model extractor supports arrival-curve based models in the form of request-bound functions (RBFs).

The RBF of a task denotes, for a particular interval length, the maximum cumulative requirement of jobs that have their arrivals within the interval [2]. This requirement being, in our context, processor time. The supply-bound function (SBF) is similar, but denotes the minimum resource supply available to the task for a particular interval length [5,6]. Earlier examples of these concepts, not necessarily under these names, can be found in real-time calculus [7].

RBFs and SBFs allow the analysis of tasks whose traces do not exhibit a predictable pattern. Specifically, the result of subtracting the RBF of a task from its SBF is another SBF describing the residual supply available to lower-priority tasks. This last SBF can be interpreted as a function that bounds the time needed in the worst case to obtain a certain amount of processor time. We can compute such a response-time bound function for any trace regardless of the timing behavior.

div.head: D. Preliminary evaluation of the period extraction
div.p: Finally, we discuss the preliminary results on the time needed by the period extractor to output an exact period. We ran the period extractor on a set of synthetic traces generated with periods {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000}ms, which are commonly encountered in automotive systems [8]. The traces were divided into 13 groups with increasing ratios between jitter and period (relative jitter), ranging from 0 to 0.999. For each relative jitter, we generated 50 traces, and recorded the error w.r.t. ground truth by extracting a model each time a new arrival was added to a trace, up to a length of 10 4 arrivals. J max was set to one second. In Fig. 3, we show for each trace (grouped by relative jitter) the time at which the error reached zero (perfect convergence).

To obtain the time, we multiplied the period of the trace by the number of samples needed for perfect convergence. Intuitively, the procedure takes longer to converge as the relative jitter grows, thus delaying the convergence point. With relative jitter set to 0.999, it took on average 8.9 seconds to reach perfect convergence, and 239 seconds in the worst case. The absolute highest observed convergence was achieved in 299 seconds, with relative jitter set to 0.8.

div.head: IV. CONCLUSION
div.p: To-date, DMXTRACE has a working RUST implementation that, starting from scheduling events recorded with FTRACE, identifies periodic workloads subject to release jitter and derives RBFs and response-time bounds for each real-time thread in the system. Going forward, we plan to extend the tool to support more models and to derive heuristics to detect elided arrivals, along with an extensive evaluation of our approach.
